title: A mobile EEG study on the psychophysiological effects of walking and crowding in indoor and outdoor urban environments
research_question: To examine the psychophysiological effects of physical (outdoor or indoor) and social (crowded versus uncrowded) urban environments in healthy young adults, to validate the use of mobile EEG and EDA measurements during active walking, and to understand how active walking influences psychological and neurophysiological responses to these environments.

participants.description: Healthy young adults (20 female; mean age 22.3, range 19-32 years) from Singapore. Participants were right-handed with normal or corrected-to-normal vision. 6 EEG datasets and 8 EDA datasets were excluded due to technical issues.
participants.recruitment: Advertisements on an online portal for research studies and serendipitous methods.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Six 1-minute (64s including fade-in/out) first-person walk-through videos of urban walkways, projected onto a wall. Environments included: green space (Gr), urban indoor crowded (IC), urban outdoor crowded (OC), urban indoor uncrowded (IU), and urban outdoor uncrowded (OU). Green space and urban environments were each presented twice.

measures.instrument: Mobile EEG (8-12.5 Hz from frontal electrodes F3, F4, F7, F8, FP1, FP2, AFz, Fz)
Mobile EEG (4-7.5 Hz from Fz and AFz)
Mobile EEG (log alpha F4 - log alpha F3)

mechanisms: Restorative effects of nature reduce attentional demands and physiological stress.
Spatial characteristics like openness, boundary height, and enclosure influence emotional and cognitive responses.
Excessive social stimulation, lack of control, and cognitive overload contribute to negative psychological effects of crowding.
Physical activity (walking) may shift affective processing of environments and influence attention allocation.
Walking may mitigate negative effects of crowding by providing a sense of agency or control.
People subconsciously require less peri-personal space in outdoor compared to indoor settings.
Outdoor environments, compared to indoor, improve executive functioning due to spatial attributes like openness and sky view.
Cognitive complexity associated with crowding acts as a distractor effect, recruiting more attentional resources.
moderators: Environment type (green, urban indoor, urban outdoor)
implementation_implications: Urban planning should consider the psychological effects of different urban environments beyond the nature-urban dichotomy.
Understanding the interaction between active movement, social density, and environment type is crucial for designing public spaces.
The findings encourage additional research into more types of urban environments and the influence of different levels of human activity.

limitations: The experimental setup used a small number of stimuli, limiting the range of environments presented.
Treadmill-walking attentional demands are lower than actual walking, potentially leading to less pronounced differences between groups.
Cultural factors and individual preferences may have influenced how crowds were appraised.
Practical constraints prevented filming crowds in green environments, limiting understanding of social influence in nature.
The effect of walking on subjective experience and appraisal of environments could only be studied in a between-subjects analysis.

paper_metadata.title: A mobile EEG study on the psychophysiological effects of walking and crowding in indoor and outdoor urban environments
paper_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_title: A mobile EEG study on the psychophysiological effects of walking and crowding in indoor and outdoor urban environments
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractEnvironmental psychologists have established multiple psychological benefits of interaction with natural, compared to urban, environments on emotion, cognition, and attention. Yet, given the increasing urbanisation worldwide, it is equally important to understand how differences within different urban environments influence human psychological experience. We developed a laboratory experiment to examine the psychophysiological effects of the physical (outdoor or indoor) and social (crowded versus uncrowded) environment in healthy young adults, and to validate the use of mobile electroencephalography (EEG) and electrodermal activity (EDA) measurements during active walking. Participants (N = 42) were randomly assigned into a walking or a standing group, and watched six 1-min walk-through videos of green, urban indoor and urban outdoor environments, depicting high or low levels of social density. Self-reported emotional states show that green spaces is perceived as more calm and positive, and reduce attentional demands. Further, the outdoor urban space is perceived more positively than the indoor environment. These findings are consistent with earlier studies on the psychological benefits of nature and confirm the effectiveness of our paradigm and stimuli. In addition, we hypothesised that even short-term exposure to crowded scenes would have negative psychological effects. We found that crowded scenes evoked higher self-reported arousal, more negative self-reported valence, and recruited more cognitive and attentional resources. However, in walking participants, they evoked higher frontal alpha asymmetry, suggesting more positive affective responses. Furthermore, we found that using recent signal-processing methods, the EEG data produced a comparable signal-to-noise ratio between walking and standing, and that despite differences between walking and standing, skin-conductance also captured effectively psychophysiological responses to stimuli. These results suggest that emotional responses to visually presented stimuli can be measured effectively using mobile EEG and EDA in ambulatory settings, and that there is complex interaction between active walking, the social density of urban spaces, and direct and indirect affective responses to such environments.
